 1          Plaintiffs Elijah Ziskin and Camila Montoya, individually and on behalf of similarly

 2   situated individuals, bring this class action suit for damages and equitable relief against Specialized

 3   Bicycle Components, Inc. (“Defendant” or “Specialized”). Plaintiffs allege the following based

 4   upon personal information as to allegations regarding themselves and the investigation of their

 5   counsel, and on information and belief as to all other allegations.

 6                                      NATURE OF THE ACTION

 7          1.      Specialized designs, manufactures, imports, and sells bicycles, bicycle parts and

 8   components, and bicycle accessories to consumers ranging from hobbyists to elite cyclists.

 9          2.      Beginning in February 2025, President Trump issued a series of executive orders

10   invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (“IEEPA”) to impose new and

11   significant tariffs (“subject tariffs”) on imports from nearly every foreign country, including those

12   from which Specialized sources its products.

13          3.      Following the imposition of the subject tariffs, Specialized publicly stated that it

14   would implement price increases across its product lines to manage the financial impact of the

15   subject tariffs. Consistent with these statements, Specialized increased the retail prices for its

16   products in the United States to account for the cost of the newly imposed tariffs. Plaintiffs and the

17   Class purchased Specialized products after these price increases took effect and, as a result, paid

18   higher prices reflecting these tariff-related adjustments (“tariff surcharges”).

19          4.      At the same time, Specialized challenged the legality of the subject tariffs in the

20   United States Court of International Trade, seeking to halt enforcement of the tariff orders and

21   obtain refunds of the duties it paid because of the subject tariffs.

22          5.      In demanding a refund for duties paid because of the subject tariffs, Specialized did

23   not acknowledge that it had passed on the economic burden of those duties onto consumers through

24   the tariff-specific adjustments. The case before the Court of International Trade was stayed pending

25   the Supreme Court’s resolution of V.O.S. Selections, Inc. v. Trump, in which businesses challenged

26   the lawfulness of the subject tariffs.

27

28

 1          6.      On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court held that the subject tariffs were unlawful.

 2   Learning Res., Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. ___, Nos. 24-1287, 25-250, 2026 WL 477534, at *13–14

 3   (U.S. Feb. 20, 2026). On remand, the Court of International Trade directed CBP to refund all IEEPA

 4   duties that were collected.

 5          7.      Despite seeking and now being entitled to a refund of the duties collected as a result

 6   of the subject tariffs, Specialized has not refunded the tariff surcharges it collected from consumers.

 7   Upon the determination that the subject tariffs were unlawful, giving rise to Specialized’s right to

 8   receive the duties it paid under the unlawful tariff scheme, Specialized was likewise obligated to

 9   return the corresponding tariff surcharge it collected from Plaintiffs and Class members.

10   Specialized’s retention of those surcharges unjustly profits Specialized at the expense of

11   consumers.

12          8.      Accordingly, Plaintiffs, on behalf of themselves and the estimated tens or hundreds

13   of thousands of similarly situated consumers, seek to ensure that their and the proposed Classes’

14   contributions to paying the subject tariffs are returned and to demand appropriate monetary,

15   equitable, injunctive, and declaratory relief.

16                                                    PARTIES

17   I.     PLAINTIFFS

18          9.      Plaintiff Elijah Ziskin is a Colorado resident. On February 2, 2026, Ziskin purchased

19   a Specialized bicycle from a Specialized authorized independent dealer in Denver, Colorado.

20   Plaintiff Ziskin was charged an increased price for his purchase that included the tariff surcharge

21   Specialized imposed.

22          10.     Plaintiff Camila Montoya is a Texas resident. On January 11, 2026, Montoya

23   purchased a Specialized bicycle from a Specialized retail store in Austin, Texas. Plaintiff Montoya

24   was charged an increased price for her purchase that included the tariff surcharge Specialized

25   imposed.

26

 1   II.     DEFENDANT

 2           11.     Defendant Specialized Bicycle Components, Inc. is a privately held company

 3   incorporated under the laws of Delaware. Specialized’s principal place of business is located at

 4   15130 Concord Circle, Morgan Hill, California, 95037.

 5           12.     Specialized Bicycle Components, Inc. markets, distributes, and sells its products to

 6   consumers throughout the United States, including within this District.

 7           13.     At all times relevant to this Complaint, Specialized was authorized to conduct and

 8   conducted business in the State of California, and regularly marketed, distributed, and sold its

 9   products to consumers throughout the United States, including in this District.

10                                             JURISDICTION

11           14.     This Court has subject matter jurisdiction pursuant to the Class Action Fairness Act,

12   28 U.S.C. § 1332(d)(2), because this is a class action where the amount in controversy exceeds the

13   sum or value of $5 million, exclusive of interest and costs, there are more than 100 putative

14   members in the proposed class, and at least one Class Member (e.g., Plaintiffs) is a citizen of a state

15   different from any Defendant.

16           15.     The Court also has supplemental jurisdiction over the state law claims pursuant to

17   28 U.S.C. § 1367 because all claims alleged are part of the same case or controversy.

18           16.     The Court has personal jurisdiction over Specialized Bicycle Components, Inc.

19   because it’s principal place of business is in this district. The Court also has personal jurisdiction

20   over Specialized Bicycle Components, Inc. because it committed the acts alleged herein in

21   California, regularly conducts business in this District, and has extensive contacts with this forum,

22   including by selling and shipping its products to consumers in this District.

23           17.     Venue is proper in this Court pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1391 because a substantial

24   part of the events or omissions giving rise to the claim occurred in this District and Defendant

25   transacts substantial business in this District.

 1                                       FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

 2             18.    Specialized is a global bicycle and cycling company that designs, manufactures,

 3   imports, and sells bicycles, bicycle frames, components, apparel, footwear and accessories. 1

 4   Specialized operates across the entire bicycle industry including designing, manufacturing,

 5   importing, and retailing its products.

 6             19.    By its own admission, Specialized is an importer of merchandise into the United

 7   States subject to the challenged subject tariffs described below.2

 8             20.    Specialized owns and controls direct-to-consumer retail storefronts and e-commerce

 9   outlets for its products, including, company-owned Specialized retail stores across the United States

10   and its direct-to-consumer e-commerce platform at specialized.com.3

11             21.    Specialized also sells its products through a network of authorized independent

12   bicycle dealers and Specialized Concept Stores throughout the United States, through which it

13   distributes its products nationwide.4 Specialized designates which bicycle dealers are “Authorized

14   Specialized Dealers,” controls this designation, and can revoke this designation at will.

15             22.    Specialized directly controls retail pricing at Authorized Specialized Dealers

16   through its Manufacturer’s Suggested Retail Price, or MSRP, structure. Specialized unilaterally

17   sets and publishes MSRP for its products.

18             23.    In Specialized’s case, the Manufacturer’s Suggested Retail Prices is, in fact, not a

19   suggestion. Specialized exercises control over the prices at which its products are advertised and

20   sold at its Authorized Specialized Dealers through a Minimum Advertised Price (“MAP”) policy.5

 3              28.   The executive order directed at Mexico imposed an additional 25 percent tariff on

 4   the import of goods from Mexico.10

 5              29.   The executive order directed at Canada imposed a 25 percent tariff on the import of

 7              30.   The executive order directed at China imposed an additional 10 percent ad valorem

 3   II.        SPECIALIZED CHARGED CONSUMERS MORE BECAUSE OF THESE

 4              TARIFFS.

 5              33.   Although they may be nominally directed extraterritorially, the increased costs

 6   created by the subject tariffs are borne almost entirely by U.S. importers and consumers. 17 The

 7   Dallas Federal Reserve concluded that the subject tariffs materially increased consumer prices and

 8   that the “pass-through from the 2025 tariffs is effectively complete.”18 In other words, that the costs

 9   of subject tariffs were ultimately borne exclusively by consumers.

10              34.   While importers must pay the subject tariffs at the border, wholesalers,

11   manufacturers, and retailers all face a choice: whether to absorb the burden of the subject tariffs or

12   to pass that burden on to their customers.19 In most cases, including in the case of Specialized, the

13   burden of tariffs is eventually passed on to U.S. consumers through retail price increases.20

14              35.   In a May 2025 survey of businesses in the New York-New Jersey region conducted

15   by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, three-quarters of both manufacturing and service

16   businesses facing tariff-induced cost increases reported they passed along at least some of these

17   higher costs to their customers by raising prices.21 Among those businesses, 40% of manufacturers

 7   Specialized’s consumers to pay a higher price for those products to cover the costs of the tariffs.

 8   This is especially the case because Specialized, as manufacturer, importer, distributer, and retailer,

 9   has control over every aspect of the pricing for its products whether through direct sales or through

10   its agreements with independent authorized dealers.

11          43.     Specialized’s tariff surcharges were designed to pass the costs resulting from the

12   subject tariffs on to consumers via increased product prices.

13          44.     Plaintiffs and each member of the Class purchased one or more of Specialized’s

14   products after the subject tariffs were imposed. At that time, Plaintiffs and the Class paid tariff

15   surcharges to Specialized through the purchase of Specialized’s products either directly or at the

16   Authorized Specialized Dealers.

18          45.     In April 2025, several companies sued in the Court of International Trade

19   challenging the legality of President Trump’s executive orders and the resulting tariffs

20   (“Challenged Tariff Orders”). 29 That Court held the Challenged Tariff Orders were unlawful

21   because they exceeded the President’s authority under the IEEPA, granted declaratory relief that

22   the Challenged orders were invalid as contrary to law, and issued a universal permanent injunction

23   enjoining enforcement of the tariffs.

 5             52.    On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court of the United States held that the subject

 6   tariffs are unlawful because the imposition of such tariffs exceeds President’s authority under the

 7   IEEPA. Learning Res., 2026 WL 477534, at *13–14. In so doing, the Supreme Court affirmed the

 8   judgment of the Court of Appeals in V.O.S. Selections, Inc., 149 F.4th 1312. Given this

 9   unappealable decision, there is now no ambiguity as to the unlawfulness of the subject tariffs. And

10   as Justice Kavanaugh noted in his dissent, “the interim effects of the Court’s decision could be

11   substantial,” including requiring the United States to “refund billions of dollars to importers who

12   paid the [subject] tariffs, even though some importers may have already passed on costs to

13   consumers or other.” Learning Res., Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. ___, Nos. 24-1287, 25-250, 2026 WL

14   477534, at *51 (U.S. Feb. 20, 2026) (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting).

15             53.    On April 17, 2026, following remand, the Court of International Trade directed CBP

16   to (1) liquidate any unliquidated entries that were subject to IEEPA duties without applying those

17   duties, and (2) reliquidate without IEEPA duties any liquidated entries for which liquidation is not

18   yet final. This means CBP must refund all IEEPA duties that were collected.
